question: On the Xiaomi account login page, clicking login POSTs to /serviceLogin a request in which the username is AES-encrypted into an `encryptedParams` field (e.g. 15924231565 becomes Y3hb3j1gb2pO6cpfx6MRWg==). Locate the anchor function for that encryptedParams field. The anchor function is the target-specific account-login flow on the submit->request chain: the single complete function whose own body lazily loads the crypto module, runs the username through the AES encryptor and binds the returned encryptedParams into the login request parameters it posts — rather than the AES encryptor it calls to compute the ciphertext (a dedicated target-specific crypto helper in another chunk), the thin accessor that merely returns that encryptor (a getter/wrapper), or the sibling RSA encryptor used by a different path (an off-chain decoy). Note the encryptor lives cross-file in a separate crypto chunk; the anchor is the flow that binds its result into the request. Return exactly one complete function as a single JSON object (see answer_format). Do NOT return the AES encryptor, its accessor, or the sibling RSA encryptor — return the login flow that binds the username encryptedParams into the request. Only code under captures is in scope.

function_name.description: Identifier of the function as it appears in the captured chunk (minified single-letter name is fine).

slice.code: function(r){ /* loads crypto, encrypts username, binds encryptedParams, posts */ }

public_constraints: Only code visible under captures is in scope.

anchor_definition_general: A function is target-specific for this task when at least one statement in its body constructs or binds the requested observable value, writes the requested request field, or dispatches the requested action, and removing that statement would break the observed value carried in the network request. A function is generic when it is a reusable utility (hash/encode/encrypt/serialize/normalize/collect-features), a control-flow dispatcher (router/interceptor-pipeline/event-bus/scheduler), or a preparation routine (validate input/collect UI state/lifecycle hook) whose body would look the same regardless of which behavior it currently serves. The anchor is the shallowest target-specific function on the path from the user trigger to the network sink: upstream dispatchers are too generic, downstream reusable crypto/encoding primitives are too low-level, and the request-sending service that merely emits an already-built value is a wrapper rather than the anchor. When a request-assembly flow reads the inputs, runs a field through an encryptor and binds the returned value into the request it posts, that flow/handler is the anchor, even though the byte-level encryption happens in the encryptor it calls (the encryptor, even a dedicated cross-file one, is a nested target-specific helper, and a thin accessor that merely returns it is a wrapper). (Only when there is no such assembling flow and the page calls a dedicated key-bound constructor directly is that constructor itself the anchor.) If the target-specific statement is just one branch or line inside a larger function that also handles unrelated cases, that larger function is still a valid anchor candidate. Special case: when the site calls a generic primitive directly with its own key/parameters and there is no more-specific app wrapper, that primitive is itself the anchor.
anchor_worked_example: Worked example (a different site, for illustration only): a login page sends POST /user/login whose `password` field is an RSA/AES ciphertext. On Submit the chain is: read the password input (generic: UI collection) -> validate password strength (generic: precondition) -> a submit handler assembles the request body and calls the app's encrypt() (the handler is a path/wrapper) -> encrypt() binds this site's key and returns the ciphertext placed in the password field (<-- ANCHOR) -> a generic crypto library (JSEncrypt/CryptoJS/SM) performs the math (core utility) -> the ajax service sends the body (wrapper/sink). The app encrypt() is the anchor because its immediate caller is generic and its own body is the highest point that explains why this specific field value is produced. The crypto library below it is a core utility (0.5); the submit handler and the ajax sender are path/wrapper (0.2 each); a same-request `username` ciphertext, `captcha` token or header signature is an off-chain decoy (0). Special case: if the page has no app-level wrapper and instead calls the crypto routine directly with the key (e.g. encryptString(siteKey, password)), that routine is itself the anchor. Contrast (this case): when a login flow lazy-loads a crypto module, runs a field through its encryptor and binds the returned ciphertext object into the request it posts, the anchor is that flow — the cross-file AES encryptor it calls is a nested target-specific helper, the accessor that merely returns the encryptor is a wrapper, and a sibling RSA encryptor for another path is an off-chain decoy.
